title: Proxy Pattern
oneLiner: Stands in for a real object, controlling, deferring, or logging access to it without the caller knowing the difference.

hero.name: Gatekeeper
hero.catchphrase: Nothing gets to the real object without going through me first.
hero.power: Impersonates the real object perfectly, adding access control, caching, or lazy loading transparently in front of it.
hero.weakness: A proxy that doesn't perfectly mimic the real object's contract — timing, errors, edge cases — becomes a subtle source of bugs that are hard to trace back to 'oh, it's the proxy'.
hero.origin: Gatekeeper was summoned after a dashboard loaded every full-resolution profile image on page load, even the 400 that were never scrolled into view.

story.problem: A profile page loads all 400 full-resolution avatar images immediately, even though the user only ever scrolls past 12 of them. Bandwidth and load time both suffer badly.
story.solution: Gatekeeper stands in as an `ImageProxy` implementing the same `Image` interface. It only loads the real, heavy image the first time `display()` is actually called — never before.
story.result: Only the images the user actually scrolls to ever load. The rest stay as lightweight proxies until (and unless) they're needed.

before: All 400 images load immediately, regardless of visibility
Bandwidth and load time paid upfront for unseen content
No way to intercept or control access to the image
after: Images load lazily, only when actually displayed
Bandwidth is paid only for what's actually viewed
The proxy can add caching, logging, or access checks transparently

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A network tab shows 400 full-resolution images loading on page load, most never seen.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: We're downloading 200MB of avatars the user will never scroll to. The page takes eight seconds to load.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: Gatekeeper stands in front of the real image, holding up a hand.
panels.speaker: Gatekeeper
panels.dialogue: Don't load the real thing yet. Let me stand in its place — I'll fetch it the moment it's actually needed, and not a second before.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: ImageProxy implements the same Image interface. display() lazily fetches the real image on first call.
panels.speaker: Gatekeeper
panels.dialogue: Callers can't tell me apart from the real image — same interface. I just don't do the expensive work until display() is actually invoked.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: Only the 12 visible avatars ever fetch their real image. Page load drops from eight seconds to under one.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: We didn't change a single line of the rendering code — just swapped in proxies. Load time dropped 8x.

useWhen: You want to defer expensive object creation until it's actually needed (virtual proxy / lazy loading).
You need to add access control, logging, or caching in front of an object without changing its interface (protection or caching proxy).
The real object lives remotely (a network service) and you want a local stand-in that handles the communication (remote proxy).
avoidWhen: The object is cheap to create and access — a proxy adds indirection with no real benefit.
You can't guarantee the proxy behaves identically to the real object in every edge case (timing, errors), risking subtle bugs.
The added indirection would make debugging significantly harder for a marginal gain.
commonMistakes: Building a proxy that doesn't perfectly match the real object's interface and error behavior, causing bugs that only show up 'through' the proxy.
Forgetting to invalidate a caching proxy, silently serving stale data forever.
Using a proxy for access control but leaving the real object independently reachable (some other code path bypasses the proxy).
Confusing Proxy (same interface, controls access) with Decorator (same interface, adds behavior) — the intents differ even when the shape looks similar.
explanation.realWorldExample: ORMs' lazy-loaded relations (a placeholder object that fetches from the database only when a field is accessed), JavaScript's built-in `Proxy` object, API gateways / rate limiters standing in front of real services, and virtual DOM diffing are all Proxy in practice.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: How is this different from Decorator? Both wrap an object behind the same interface.

conversation.speaker: Gatekeeper
conversation.message: Decorator ADDS behavior to something already accessible. I CONTROL whether — and when — you reach the real thing at all: lazy loading, access checks, caching.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: What breaks if the proxy isn't careful?

conversation.speaker: Gatekeeper
conversation.message: If I don't behave EXACTLY like the real object — same errors, same timing contract — callers get bugs they can't explain, because as far as they know, they're just talking to the real thing.

codeBattle.scenario: Your app calls a third-party geocoding API that charges per request and rate-limits aggressively. The same addresses get looked up repeatedly across the app.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: Gatekeeper can sit in front of the real geocoding client as a caching proxy, serving repeated lookups from cache and only hitting the real API — and the rate limit — when truly necessary.

quiz.question: What does a Proxy do that distinguishes it from a plain wrapper?
options: It implements the exact same interface as the real object and controls access to it — lazily, securely, or with caching
It always changes the interface of the object it wraps
It permanently replaces the real object
It requires the real object to be a Singleton
quiz.answer: It implements the exact same interface as the real object and controls access to it — lazily, securely, or with caching
quiz.explanation: Matching the real object's interface exactly is what lets a proxy stand in transparently.

quiz.question: What is a 'virtual proxy' used for?
options: Deferring expensive object creation until it's actually needed
Translating one interface into another incompatible one
Adding new behavior permanently to every instance of a class
quiz.answer: Deferring expensive object creation until it's actually needed
quiz.explanation: Virtual proxies delay the expensive work (like loading a full-resolution image) until the moment it's genuinely required.

quiz.question: How does Proxy differ from Decorator?
options: Proxy controls whether/when you reach the real object; Decorator adds behavior to an object you already have full access to
They are identical patterns under different names
Decorator can only be used with remote objects
Proxy always makes code faster, Decorator always makes it slower
quiz.answer: Proxy controls whether/when you reach the real object; Decorator adds behavior to an object you already have full access to
quiz.explanation: The structural shape is similar, but the intent differs: access control versus behavior extension.

quiz.question: What's the biggest risk of a poorly-implemented Proxy?
options: It doesn't perfectly replicate the real object's behavior and errors, causing bugs that are hard to trace back to the proxy
It always uses more memory than the real object
It prevents the real object from ever being created
It requires rewriting every caller of the real object
quiz.answer: It doesn't perfectly replicate the real object's behavior and errors, causing bugs that are hard to trace back to the proxy
quiz.explanation: Because callers believe they're talking to the real object, any behavioral mismatch in the proxy becomes a confusing, hidden bug.
